title: The Axiomatic Principle of Necessarily Indefinite Containment
deck:
Any dimensionally finite structure would require another structure
            beyond it, producing an indefinite hierarchy of containment.

concise.body:
Chapter

The Axiomatic Principle of Necessarily Indefinite Containment, proposed by TUIDG, is intrinsic to a supposed structural element with a quantified dimension.

This logical, axiomatic principle makes it evident that there cannot be an uncontained structural element, implying that if there were a dimensionally finite universe, or even infinite dimensionally finite universes, it would be necessary for something external to exist that would contain them and which, by consequence, would be something dimensionally infinite.

The Problematic of Ideas

Since humanity began seeking to understand the fundamental questions concerning the universe across diverse fields of knowledge, countless theoretical models have been created to explain the supposed origin of its micro- and macro-structures, either separately or as a whole.

According to the first hypothesis, the universe "Has Always Existed," and from there, it could develop in the following sub-modes: Continuous and Static or Discontinuous and Dynamic.

If the universe Has Always Existed in a Continuous and Static mode, its essential microstructure would have palpable reality—it would have materiality—but a materiality that would be continuous, therefore rigid, incorruptible, immobile, and could neither be created nor destroyed.

Conversely, according to the second hypothesis, it "Began to Exist," in two distinct sub-modes: From Something or From Nothing.

If it Began to Exist From Nothing, then it would have the possibility of being in any of the previous modes, for following the eventual creation (by God), the probable paths through which it could "evolve" could only be the same.

If matter were continuous, the universe would necessarily have to be full—that is, there should be no voids between such "being"; it would be an absolutely dense universe, immobile, and without distinctions between things, therefore without relations, without reciprocity, and without any attributes.

If it were discontinuous, it should then be a mixture of being and non-being—that is, there should exist an absolute void and material corpuscles dissolved within it, for only this void could guarantee the mobility of these corpuscles.

In this conception, these corpuscles possess a minimum and maximum dimensional limit, as does the structure of this type of universe itself, despite the logical possibility that fundamental particles could be divided indefinitely, and despite the unrestricted possibility of the existence of a void with an absolutely infinite dimension surrounding a finite material universe.

What Is the Shape of the Universe?

This question only makes sense to physicists who adhere to the Standard Cosmological Model (SCM), as they genuinely believe the universe arose through a great explosion ridiculously called the "Big Bang." However, if approached from a philosophical and rational perspective, the most logical answer is that the universe has no shape, for only that which is finite possesses a shape, and the One is necessarily infinite.

According to the Standard Cosmological Model, the universe could have one of three possible shapes when viewed from "outside," depending on the ratio of the average density of matter to the average density of energy—the "density parameter omega" ($\Omega$):

If omega were greater than 1 ($\Omega > 1$), we would have a spherical universe or one of "positive curvature," such that "space" would be spherical and finite, like a soccer ball.

If omega were less than 1 ($\Omega < 1$), we would have a hyperbolic universe or one of "negative curvature," such that "space" would resemble a saddle.

If omega were equal to 1 ($\Omega = 1$), we would have a flat universe or one of "neutral curvature," such that "space" would be Euclidean.

Now, returning to the logical reality of the universe according to the propositions of TUIDG, there are no "non-Euclidean geometries"; all geometry is one, call it what you will.

What kind of shape could a universe assume if it were the result of a "great explosion," where all matter, energy, and space itself were concentrated into an infinite point that inexplicably came to expand at an accelerated rate in a Big Bang?

Would it be, today, a type of sphere where its elements were distributed in a practically homogeneous manner throughout its volume?

In every type of explosion, all "particles," "atoms," and molecules, in the form of hot gases and light, are expelled in all directions.

Thus, for a post-Big Bang universe in formation, taking gravity into account, it would be logical to suppose that—as happens with the dynamics of supernova formation (which form a "remnant core" of the star, resulting from the equilibrium between the expansive force produced by nuclear fusion and the star's gravity)—a similar process would occur.

Now, we can imagine that galaxies and everything we know are contained within this rapidly expanding membrane, with or without a remnant core of gigantic proportions in its interior.

Regarding the direction of expansion (outward): if the thickness of the membrane were smaller than the Hubble volume, we would see, in a sequence of layers, something like a cosmic horizon constituted by the first objects formed, expanded, and ejected by the singularity.

Regarding the perpendicular to the direction of expansion (up or down): with the membrane thickness smaller than the Hubble volume, we would see cosmic objects that are much more distant.

This entire explanation proposes to make it understood that if the universe had arisen from a primordial singularity—if there had truly been a Big Bang—this universe, in this mold and with these dynamics, would be, at the very least, structurally different from the universe we know and of which we are a part.

full.body:
Chapter

The Axiomatic Principle of Necessarily Indefinite Containment, proposed by TUIDG, is intrinsic to a supposed structural element with a quantified dimension. It establishes the impossibility of the existence of a "structural element" not contained by another "structural element," implying that if there were a "dimensionally finite universe"—or even "infinite dimensionally finite universes"—it would be necessary for there to be something external to these "finite universes" that would contain them and which, by "infinite consequence," would necessarily be "something infinite."

This logical, axiomatic principle makes it evident that there cannot be an uncontained structural element, implying that if there were a dimensionally finite universe, or even infinite dimensionally finite universes, it would be necessary for something external to exist that would contain them and which, by consequence, would be something dimensionally infinite. This dimensionally infinite "something" is, obviously, a common infinite space—a common infinite place that could contain the eventual infinite universes—but which, according to the propositions of TUIDG, is the one and only infinite universe, being solely an Absolute Empty Space called the Omega Dimension.

The Problematic of Ideas

Since humanity began seeking to understand the fundamental questions concerning the universe across diverse fields of knowledge, countless theoretical models have been created to explain the supposed origin of its micro- and macro-structures, either separately or as a whole. However, these ideological conceptions used to explain the existence of the universe—whether in the philosophical, religious, or scientific fields—rely, in the final analysis, on only two fundamental hypotheses: the one that maintains that the universe Has Always Existed and the one that maintains that it Began to Exist. Each, however, possesses distinct sub-modes of being, as shown in the hierarchical diagram.

According to the first hypothesis, the universe "Has Always Existed," and from there, it could develop in the following sub-modes: Continuous and Static or Discontinuous and Dynamic.

If the universe Has Always Existed in a Continuous and Static mode, its essential microstructure would have palpable reality—it would have materiality—but a materiality that would be continuous, therefore rigid, incorruptible, immobile, and could neither be created nor destroyed. It would thus be infinite in time and space, for as it has always existed, it would make no sense for it to be contained by an Absolute Empty Space.

If the universe Has Always Existed in a Discontinuous and Dynamic mode, its essential microstructure would also have palpable reality—it would have materiality—but it would be corpuscular, therefore mobile, yet also incorruptible (as it would make no sense for it to be different from itself), as well as infinite in time and space, for the same reasons as above.

Conversely, according to the second hypothesis, it "Began to Exist," in two distinct sub-modes: From Something or From Nothing.

If the universe Began to Exist From Something, it could have evolved in two sub-modes: Discontinuous, Dynamic, and Cyclic (DD C)—that is, with a corpuscular, real, mobile, but corruptible structure, where the entire structure evolves to a certain point, then collapses and returns in a new beginning with potentially new and different structures, but always starting from an initial "Something"—or it Began to Exist from Something in a Discontinuous, Dynamic, and Linear (DD L) mode, having all the characteristics of the previous hypothesis, but being infinite in time.

If it Began to Exist From Nothing, then it would have the possibility of being in any of the previous modes, for following the eventual creation (by God), the probable paths through which it could "evolve" could only be the same. Note that these assertions regarding the eventual "evolutionary paths" of the universe do not require a posteriori justifications; they do not require direct or indirect observations, but rather only a priori ones, through the nature of reason. According to TUIDG, if materiality truly existed, it could be either continuous or discontinuous, the latter being a mixture of materiality and immateriality, of being and non-being.

If matter were continuous, the universe would necessarily have to be full—that is, there should be no voids between such "being"; it would be an absolutely dense universe, immobile, and without distinctions between things, therefore without relations, without reciprocity, and without any attributes. Such a universe would be merely an infinitely dense block with infinite Structural Dimension. But accepting real materiality instead of immateriality makes a universe with such characteristics logically inconceivable.

If it were discontinuous, it should then be a mixture of being and non-being—that is, there should exist an absolute void and material corpuscles dissolved within it, for only this void could guarantee the mobility of these corpuscles. At first, this mode of being seems logically possible when real materiality is accepted; however, we will see throughout this theory that it is inconsistent. The idea of a full universe was, unfortunately, abandoned; yet, in essence, it is the one that leads to the path of the true universal structure, but only when one rejects real materiality. The idea of a non-full universe, which currently prevails, is based on indivisible fundamental corpuscles as the formative principle of its supposed materiality; however, this conception—according to TUIDG’s propositions—is what leads to the path of deception and contradiction regarding the structure and functionality of the cosmos.

In this conception, these corpuscles possess a minimum and maximum dimensional limit, as does the structure of this type of universe itself, despite the logical possibility that fundamental particles could be divided indefinitely, and despite the unrestricted possibility of the existence of a void with an absolutely infinite dimension surrounding a finite material universe. Models along this line, however, are those that have gained the most followers. In this context, the most sophisticated is the standard cosmological model, governed by the insane assumptions of quantum mechanics and special and general relativity, which is nothing more than a probability model filled with uncertainties and inconsistencies. Nevertheless, regarding the types, modes, and forms of being, according to TUIDG’s logic, the universe is nothing more than something absolutely empty, immobile, and dimensionally infinite, whose fundamental structures are formed by immaterial and dimensionless geometric elements, formed by an Immaterial Geometry.

What Is the Shape of the Universe?

This question only makes sense to physicists who adhere to the Standard Cosmological Model (SCM), as they genuinely believe the universe arose through a great explosion ridiculously called the "Big Bang." However, if approached from a philosophical and rational perspective, the most logical answer is that the universe has no shape, for only that which is finite possesses a shape, and the One is necessarily infinite.

According to the Standard Cosmological Model, the universe could have one of three possible shapes when viewed from "outside," depending on the ratio of the average density of matter to the average density of energy—the "density parameter omega" ($\Omega$):

If omega were greater than 1 ($\Omega > 1$), we would have a spherical universe or one of "positive curvature," such that "space" would be spherical and finite, like a soccer ball.

If omega were less than 1 ($\Omega < 1$), we would have a hyperbolic universe or one of "negative curvature," such that "space" would resemble a saddle. Imagine a universe modeled on such an absurdity!

If omega were equal to 1 ($\Omega = 1$), we would have a flat universe or one of "neutral curvature," such that "space" would be Euclidean. It is precisely this result that physicists' "measurements" point toward.

Now, returning to the logical reality of the universe according to the propositions of TUIDG, there are no "non-Euclidean geometries"; all geometry is one, call it what you will. If there can exist more than one parallel line or if the sums of the internal angles of triangles can differ, these facts are merely a matter of the relations between geometric forms, not the space that contains them. It is the geometric forms that possess such qualities, not space itself. This conclusion is not a matter of "common sense"—as if that were something essentially flawed—but a matter of non-contradictory, logical conclusions.

What kind of shape could a universe assume if it were the result of a "great explosion," where all matter, energy, and space itself were concentrated into an infinite point that inexplicably came to expand at an accelerated rate in a Big Bang? What is the most logical mode of shape for the universe, given a dynamic scenario in which an "atom" of primordial energy—a space-time singularity—expands at the speed of light?

Would it be, today, a type of sphere where its elements were distributed in a practically homogeneous manner throughout its volume? And within that volume, would there be practically the same density and distribution of elements, even in the space where the epicenter of the explosion would have been?

Even if physicists do not wish to, or cannot, admit the logical existence of a primordial epicenter, we observe that in absolutely any type of explosion—whether that of a chemical artifact, a nuclear device, or a star—the shape that always prevails is that of a "spherical bubble" or a "spherical membrane," usually hollow, with layers of different densities formed by the debris of the explosion. These continue to grow and rarefy until any of the forces at play (gravity/pressure vs. fission/fusion) disrupt the equilibrium of their shape.

In every type of explosion, all "particles," "atoms," and molecules, in the form of hot gases and light, are expelled in all directions. Since the inner layers of the expanding "gases" are always denser and under higher pressure than the outer layers, these gases tend to move away from the epicenter. Thus, as long as the process of explosion/expansion of all matter initially contained in the body lasts, the result—as a function of the expansion velocity of the gases/matter—is the formation of a basically spherical and hollow structure, like a soap bubble with slight deformations.

Thus, for a post-Big Bang universe in formation, taking gravity into account, it would be logical to suppose that—as happens with the dynamics of supernova formation (which form a "remnant core" of the star, resulting from the equilibrium between the expansive force produced by nuclear fusion and the star's gravity)—a similar process would occur. In this case, however, the quantity of "magical" and inexplicable energy converted into "matter" would be progressively smaller and, therefore, insufficient to sustain the expansion/contraction imbalance. The dynamics of a post-Big Bang universe would not be exactly the same, but very similar to the final aspect of a supernova that is still expanding, given that in the latter case, there are gravitational forces and tensions of the interstellar vacuum that would cause the two structures to take on slightly different shapes. The relationship between their final volume and the thickness of the membrane is a function of the initial quantity of matter and energy per unit of expansion time.

Now, we can imagine that galaxies and everything we know are contained within this rapidly expanding membrane, with or without a remnant core of gigantic proportions in its interior. If we looked in all directions, what we would see would be very different from what we see today; we could not be observing its structures the way we are. What we would see from any point on this "shell" of matter would be highly relative, depending only on the observed direction and whether the thickness of the membrane were greater or smaller than the Hubble volume.

Regarding the direction of expansion (outward): if the thickness of the membrane were smaller than the Hubble volume, we would see, in a sequence of layers, something like a cosmic horizon constituted by the first objects formed, expanded, and ejected by the singularity. This would form the outermost part of this matter shell on the boundary line with the empty space into which everything would be expanding, and from which we could not obtain any type of background radiation or any information other than a type of inference about this absolute void. Regarding the direction of expansion (inward): with the membrane thickness smaller than the Hubble volume, in a sequence of layers, we would see something like a "reverse horizon," constituted by the last objects formed, expanded, and ejected by the singularity, preceded by a practically empty space, yet with dissolved matter and energy, providing a small residual energetic reading compared to the energy of the shell, the remnant core (if any) of the singularity, and the other side of the membrane, receding at double the velocity (assuming a uniform expansion velocity).

Regarding the perpendicular to the direction of expansion (up or down): with the membrane thickness smaller than the Hubble volume, we would see cosmic objects that are much more distant. Only for a certain observation angle—forming a narrow-aperture observation cone—would the Hubble volume be exceeded, making the cosmological principle valid for these observable regions—or rather, for observers positioned on these axes of observation perpendicular to the direction of expansion.

This entire explanation proposes to make it understood that if the universe had arisen from a primordial singularity—if there had truly been a Big Bang—this universe, in this mold and with these dynamics, would be, at the very least, structurally different from the universe we know and of which we are a part. And, by determination of the Axiomatic Principle of Necessarily Indefinite Containment, it would be contained by the Absolute Void. Thus, according to the principles of TUIDG, the universe has no shape, for it is dimensionally infinite.
